title: Sustainable Direct Mn Alloying Practice to Produce Medium Mn Steel
abstract: Abstract Manganese alloying via. direct reduction of MnO in ladle refining slag is a promising alternative to energy and cost intensive conventional ferroalloy production methods. This study explores the aluminothermic reduction of MnO in CaO–SiO 2 –Al 2 O 3 –MgO slag under varying CaO/SiO 2  ratios, Al 2 O 3  content, and stoichiometric addition of aluminum for 4 and 8 mass% Mn concentrations in molten iron. The results showed that the slag containing 30 mass% Al 2 O 3  suppressed Mn volatilization, whereas Al 2 O 3 -free slags exhibited a faster MnO reduction but a larger vaporization loss. On the other hand, the slag with CaO/SiO 2  ratio of 2 without second-phase precipitation, facilitating enhanced slag–metal separation and reduced metal droplet suspension, showed significant improvement in Mn recovery of 68%. Furthermore, excessive Al addition leads to higher Mn loss. An empirical equation for Mn loss was developed to correlate Mn loss with factors such as slag basicity, Al 2 O 3  content, Mn distribution ratio between slag and metal, and the amount of aluminum added. sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The demand for superior mechanical properties [ 1 ] and improving fuel efficiency by reducing the weight of auto components lead to the development and industrial adoption of Advanced High-Strength Steel (AHSS) [ 1 ,  2 ]. The 3rd-generation AHSS consists of Mn level ranging from 3 to 12% is designed to achieve a strength–elongation product exceeding 25,000 MPa, largely due to the Transformation-Induced Plasticity (TRIP) effect. Mn content in Medium Manganese Steel (MMnS) is added to stabilize the austenite phase and facilitate TRIP behavior [ 3 ]. Additionally, aluminum (Al) and silicon (Si) contributing to the light weighting of steel, are added to refine the microstructure and tailor transformation kinetics [ 4 ,  5 – 6 ].

Traditionally, Mn is added to liquid steel in the form of ferromanganese (Fe–Mn) or silicomanganese (Si–Mn) alloys. These ferro alloys are produced via carbothermic or silicothermic reduction of manganese ore in submerged arc furnaces. This process involves up to 40–70% [ 7 ] of total energy input and emits ~ 1.8 and ~ 2.8 tons of CO 2  per ton of Fe–Mn and Si–Mn, respectively [ 8 ]. Further, it is also reported that the total Mn recovery rarely exceeds 50%, losses accounting for ore dressing, smelting, and recovery during addition in the ladle [ 9 ]. Nokhrina and Rozhihina [ 9 ] reported that manganese loss was 20–25%, 20–25% and up to 25% during ore beneficiation, ferroalloy smelting, and alloying into steel, respectively. It is reported that during silicothermic smelting, 3.5–4.0 tons of slag containing up to 20–22 mass% MnO is produced per ton of metallic manganese, leads 40% of the manganese loss to the slag [ 10 ,  11 – 12 ]. In addition, since manganese vapor pressure [ 13 ] is unusually high; therefore, its evaporation during smelting and alloying is unavoidable during steelmaking.

To combat recovery losses, environmental impact, and rising alloying costs, the steel industry is currently exploring alternative alloying strategies that could improve Mn recovery, reduce carbon intensity, and enhance process efficiency. One approach is direct alloying [ 14 ,  15 ] or in-situ alloying or reductive alloying practice involves the direct addition of ores/oxides into the molten steel bath during secondary refining along with suitable reductant to recover the alloying elements such as Mn, Cr [ 16 ,  17 ,  18 – 19 ], B [ 20 ], and V [ 21 ,  22 – 23 ]. This practice is expected to circumvent the need for ferroalloys production and allows for the maximum possible recovery in the molten steel under thermodynamically favorable conditions.

Laboratory experiments on Mn direct alloying were conducted by Wen et al. [ 24 ] using SiC as a reductant in the liquid steel. The Mn yield improved with lower FeO content, slag basicity between 2 and 4, higher carbon content, and temperature, highlighting the role of slag chemistry and oxidation potential on Mn recovery. Wu et al. [ 25 ,  26 ] showed that the mass transfer of Mn in slag is the rate-limiting step at 1873 K and achieved Mn recovery in the first 1 min over 43% using mixtures of carbon, aluminum, and ferrosilicon powder as reducing agents and higher slag basicity, when fed via wire, but dropped significantly to 10.98% when top slag was added, highlighting the importance of contact efficiency in direct alloying.

Some more direct alloying studies focused on carbothermic [ 27 ,  28 ,  29 ,  30 ,  31 – 32 ] and silicothermic [ 33 ] reduction of MnO-containing slags reported sluggish kinetics and interfacial limitations [ 29 ]. Shimo et al. [ 27 ,  28 ] showed that at low MnO contents (< 8%), Mn vaporization dominates, with evaporation rate equal to reduction rate. While Ashizuka et al. [ 30 ] emphasized that increase in slag basicity (CaO/SiO 2 ) lowers the activation energy for MnO reduction. Jamieson BJ et al. [ 31 ,  33 ] identified CO nucleation at the interface of slag and metal and oxygen transport from slag as rate-controlling steps. Daines and Pehlke [ 32 ] found that interfacial reactions and Mn diffusion in metal-controlled carbothermic and silicothermic reductions, respectively.

Meanwhile, industrial-scale trials have demonstrated Mn recovery of over 90% using self-reducing ore pellets or manganese oxide addition during secondary slag removal or double-slag converter processes [ 34 ,  35 ]. Notably, Nokhrina et al. [ 36 ] proposed a two-step method for recovering Mn from MnO in Electric Arc Furnace (EAF) steelmaking, including slag removal, coke breeze addition, and silicon feeding. Similarly, Dmitrienko et al. [ 37 ] and Chen and He [ 38 ] conducted thermodynamic and kinetic models to confirm the influence of carbon, FeO, and slag volume on Mn recovery. Wang et al. [ 39 ] further demonstrated 65% Mn recovery using self-reducing ore briquettes.

Studies by Kudyba et al. [ 42 ] and Monterio et al. [ 43 ] confirmed that Al can efficiently reduce MnO from slags, [ 43 ] as its exothermicity supports open ladle reactions. Kamaraj et al. [ 44 ] have reported the Manganese recovery of 100–110% in the ladle furnace after liquid steel tapping. The excess recovery was reported due to contribution of Mn from carryover BOF slag. The HalMan process by Safarian [ 45 ] integrates the hydrogen pre-reduction of manganese ores with aluminothermic smelting to produce Mn alloys. However, its application in ladle refining remains scarcely addressed, even though slag plays a crucial role in desulfurization, deoxidation, and inclusions removal. Careful selection of the slag composition is essential to ensure a sufficiently low melting point after dissolution and reduction of Mn oxides [ 9 ,  46 ].

Several laboratory studies have investigated ladle slag–steel reactions in Al-killed steels [ 47 ,  48 ,  49 – 50 ]. Deng et al. [ 47 ] study revealed that when Mn content > 6 mass% in steel, SiO 2  from the slag can be reduced by dissolved Mn, indicating strong Mn activity gradients during refining. Also recommends that the basicity of slag should be above 4 for the processing of Mn steels. Most existing work focuses on metal desulfurization during direct alloying with manganese in the ladle at a very low Mn level of 0.5% [ 51 ].Yet, these studies [ 47 ,  48 ,  49 ,  50 – 51 ] do not address the Mn loss mechanism happens during direct alloying and refining conditions.

The present study is therefore designed to investigate the reduction of MnO from ladle furnace slags using metallic aluminum as the reductant. To better understand Mn behavior at elevated MnO levels, to examine the extent of Mn vaporization, which is not well understood, while varying the process conditions such as slag system, basicity, and stoichiometry of aluminum addition. Two industrially relevant Mn target levels, 4 mass% and 8 mass% in metal, are selected to represent medium Mn steels of 3rd-generation AHSS. To assess the influence of slag chemistry, CaO/SiO 2  ratios of 1 and 2 are chosen to simulate ladle furnace slags. In addition, to clarify the effect of reductant dosage on Mn recovery and Mn loss, aluminum was added in amounts of 1, 2, and 2.5 times the stoichiometric amount required for the reduction of MnO oxide. This systematic investigation aimed to clarify the role of slag composition, and excess Al addition in determining the efficiency of Mn alloying by the aluminothermic reduction during secondary steel refining conditions.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs:
The two synthetic slag systems composed of CaO–SiO 2 –MgO and CaO–SiO 2 –Al 2 O 3 –MgO were prepared by mixing the special grade CaCO 3 , SiO 2 , MgO, and Al 2 O 3  reagents, in a predetermined mass ratio, respectively. The mixed powder was pressed to cylindrical tablets and heated in a muffle furnace at 1223 K for 9 h to completely remove CO 2 . After cooling, the tablets were crushed, mixed with an appropriate amount of MnO, and then compressed into tablets. The chemical compositions of those mixtures are listed in Table  1  and marked by red plots in the pseudo-ternary phase diagrams at  1873 K of MnO–CaO–SiO 2  at 21 mass% MgO (MgO saturated) (Fig.  1 a) and that of MgO–CaO–SiO 2  at 30 mass% Al 2 O 3  and 3.71 mass% MnO (Fig.  1 b), which were constructed by FactSage 8.3 with FToxid, FSstel, and FT pure substances databases. In all experiments, MgO crucibles of dimensions height  40 mm, outer diameter 28 mm, and inner diameter 22 mm were used. As shown in Fig.  1 , the initial slag compositions were designed to be MgO saturated to prevent the erosion of the MgO from the working crucible by the slag melt. The viscosity of slag and activity of MnO at  1873 K, calculated using FactSage 8.3, along with the basicity of slag compositions, are given in Table  1 .

sections.heading: Results and Discussion
Effect of Al 2 O 3
paragraphs: Figure  3  shows the comparison of Mn distribution in slag and metal and losses occurred after the aluminothermic reduction of MnO present in Al 2 O 3 -free MgO-saturated slag (expt ID: 4MnC1S2.5 NAl 2 O 3 ) with the Al 2 O 3 -rich MgO-saturated slag (expt ID: 4MnC1S2.5). The recovery of Mn into metal and slag was  22.10 and 55.77%  for Al 2 O 3 -rich slag, compared to  10.37 and 50.12%  for the Al 2 O 3 -free slag, respectively. In contrast, Mn loss was significantly higher for the Al 2 O 3 -free slag than Al 2 O 3 -rich slag during the experiment .  This signifies the role of aluminate slags in suppressing the losses and favoring Mn retention in both metal and slag. It should be noted that the MnO reduction from the slag was promoted in the case of MgO-saturated Al 2 O 3 -free slag. This is attributed to the increase in the activity coefficient of MnO [ 52 ,  53 ] and decrease in the viscosity of the slag [ 42 ] (refer to Table  1 ) due to enhanced silicate structure depolymerization by O 2−  ions from MgO and CaO. Fig. 3 Distribution of Mn in slag–metal–vapor phases for 0% Al 2 O 3  and 30% Al 2 O 3  containing slags

Whereas in the case of the MgO-saturated Al 2 O 3 -rich slag, the high content of Al 2 O 3  significantly reduces the activity coefficient of MnO [ 54 ] and increases the viscosity (refer to Table  1 ). The increase in slag viscosity is primarily due to the bonding of tetrahedral units of AlO 3  anion with the tetrahedral SiO 4  anion to form a more polymerized silicate network [ 52 ]. The increase in slag viscosity, thereby inhibiting the Mn mass transfer in the slag [ 55 ]. As a result, in the slag system containing 30% Al 2 O 3 , both the reduction of (MnO) to [Mn] and the Mn evaporation flux into the gas phase are suppressed, resulting in an increased Mn retention in the slag and metal.

sections.heading: Influence of CaO/SiO 2  Ratio
paragraphs: Figure  4  shows the variation of Mn distribution in slag and metal, and losses occurred with the slags of CaO/SiO 2  mass ratios of 1 (expt ID: 4MnC1S2, 8MnC1S2) and 2 (expt ID: 4MnC2S2, 8MnC2S2). By increasing the CaO/SiO 2  mass ratio from 1 to 2, Mn recovery in metal increases from 30.07% to 68.64% for the 4% Mn target (refer to Fig.  4 a) and from 20.41% to 64.81% for the 8% Mn target (refer to Fig.  4 a). Notably, it is concluded that better Mn recovery in the metal is achieved at CaO/SiO 2  = 2. For the 4% Mn target in Fig.  4 a, the Mn loss for the slag with CaO/SiO 2  = 1 (4.47%) was lower than that with CaO/SiO 2  = 2 slag (11.26%). However, for 8% Mn target (refer to Fig.  4 b), the opposite trend for Mn loss such as the Mn loss for the slag with CaO/SiO 2  = 1 is 29.98% and for the slag with CaO/SiO 2  = 2 is 16.83%. These experimental findings can be explained with the help of SEM micrographs taken near the crucible–slag interface as shown in Fig.  5 . For the slag with CaO/SiO 2  = 1, solid phases are observed in both the 4% Mn target (Fig.  5 a) and the 8% Mn target (Fig.  5 b). Fig. 4 Distribution of Mn in slag, metal, and vapor phases at CaO/SiO 2  ratios = 1 and 2 for the slags containing 30 mass% Al 2 O 3 .  a  4% Mn target and  b  8% Mn target Fig. 5 SEM micrographs showing slag–metal–crucible interaction on the cross-section of slags at different Mn targets and CaO/SiO 2  ratios.  a  4%Mn target and  b  8%Mn target at CaO/SiO 2  = 1, and  c  4%Mn target and  d  8%Mn target at CaO/SiO 2  = 2

The solid phases observed in the slag with CaO/SiO 2  = 1 appear to have more entrapped metal droplets. The compositions of metal particles were determined using the SEM–EDS technique, and the results are presented in Table  4 . From SEM–EDS analysis (Fig.  5 ), it can also be observed that a dark contrast second phase is present in the slag phase. They are confirmed to be rich in Al and Mg through EDS mapping (Fig.  6 ). Quantitative analysis using SEM–EDS confirmed that those solid phases were spinel (MgAl 2 O 4 ) due to interaction with the crucible [ 48 ]. In the case of the 4%Mn target (Fig.  6 a), the Mn content in the metal droplets is relatively low. In contrast, for the 8%Mn target (Fig.  6 b), the entrapped metal droplets are drastically rich in Mn, as given in Table  4 . This suggests that MnO was reduced by Al and trapped in the slag as metallic manganese before dissolving into the liquid iron phase. These results show that Mn loss depends on both Mn concentration and slag basicity: at low Mn levels at basicity 2, losses occur mainly through vaporization due to the slower reduction rate, while at high-Mn levels at basicity 1, additional losses arise from the entrapment of Mn-rich droplets.

Furthermore, the presence of the solid spinel phases reduces the effective liquid fraction in the slag (see Table  5 ), thereby increasing the viscosity [ 56 ] and inhomogeneity of the slag. As reported by Shimazaki et al. [ 57 ] slags containing a large amount of solid phase (> 20 vol%) exhibit a markedly higher viscosity, slowing the terminal settling velocity of metal droplets by nearly 55%, regardless of their particle size. This increases the drag coefficient of the droplets, further hindering their separation. In contrast, for the slag with CaO/SiO 2  = 2, no spinel formation is observed, and the slag remains a homogeneous liquid (refer Fig.  5 c and d), lowering the viscosity and facilitating efficient separation of the metal droplets from slag.

It should be noted that Rafiei et al. [ 58 ] identified Mn loss mechanisms as vaporization, oxidation into slag, and evaporation–condensation in the bubble during AOD. However, the existing literature has not explicitly addressed the loss and/or recovery of Mn during direct alloying in the ladle refining stage at lower/higher Mn contents. Thus, the present investigation clarifies the Mn loss is not governed only by vapor loss but is also significantly influenced by the mass transfer kinetics within the slag phase and through the slag/metal interface for settling of metal droplets.

sections.heading: Effect of Al Additions
paragraphs: Figure  7  shows the variation of the Mn distribution in the metal and slag phase and a loss occurred with increasing aluminum addition. For all conditions except 4%Mn target at CaO/SiO 2  = 2 (Fig.  7 c), the MnO reduction obviously proceeds with increasing Al amount. At CaO/SiO 2  = 1, the addition of a stoichiometric amount of Al led to negligible Mn loss (below 0.3%) in both experiments with 4% and 8% Mn targets (Fig.  7 a and b, respectively). However, when the amount of Al was increased beyond the stoichiometric requirement, Mn loss begins to rise, especially in the 8% Mn target system. This is due to the exothermic reaction of the aluminothermic reduction, which locally raises the temperature at the slag/metal interface, with the addition of more MnO and Al. This thermal spike, coupled with increased Mn activity, could promote Mn volatilization, or change the viscosity, leading to instability and entrapment of Mn-rich metal droplets within the slag, as shown in Fig.  6 b, thereby inhibiting the Mn recovery into the bulk metal and leading to increase Mn loss. Mn evaporation acceleration at high temperatures with initial Mn contents were confirmed by Chu and Bao [ 59 ,  60 ] during vacuum refining of Mn steel. Further, they reported the gasification rate of Mn decreased from 0.0410 cm/min to 0.0192 cm/min when the melt is covered with slag. Fig. 7 Distribution of Mn in metal, slag, and vapor phase with increased Al additions for 4%Mn target at  a  CaO/SiO 2  = 1 and  c  CaO/SiO 2  = 2, and for 8%Mn target at  b  CaO/SiO 2  = 1 and  d  CaO/SiO 2  = 2

In contrast, at CaO/SiO 2  = 2, even with the stoichiometric addition of Al, apparent Mn loss (1 to 4%) was observed in Fig.  7 c and d, although the loss is still lower than those that observed at CaO/SiO 2  = 1 when excess Al was inserted. Interestingly, the Mn loss increases in the 8% Mn target case compared to the 4% Mn target, indicating that higher Mn concentrations are inherently more loss-prone, even under favorable basicity. Mn recovery into the metal improves significantly, reaching > 68% and 64% for the 4%Mn and 8%Mn targets, respectively. This behavior is due to a combination of faster separation in fully liquid slags and a higher driving force for Mn transfer due to increased MnO activity. These observations suggest that Al is an effective reductant; its amount must be carefully controlled, especially in high-Mn systems. This interpretation is consistent with industrial findings. For instance, in the VOD process of Mn steel, Sharma et al. [ 55 ] reported that the highest Mn recovery was achieved when the CaO/SiO 2  ratio was maintained at 1.5 at 1585 °C.

sections.heading: Effect of Slag Viscosity on Mn Recovery
paragraphs: Relationships between final slag viscosity calculated by the viscosity module of FactSage 8.3 (Table  3 ) and Mn distribution in the metal and vapor phases are shown in Fig.  8 . Higher slag viscosity reduces the reduction rate, thereby correlating with reduced Mn recovery and Mn losses because of reduced reduction kinetics. This means that at lower slag viscosity, loss is high, i.e., the reduced Mn in metal easily evaporates due to efficient mass transfer and faster kinetics at slag/metal interface. The viscosity range of 0.1–0.12 Pa·s (highlighted in red ellipse) yields a higher Mn recovery to the metal and reduced Mn loss. Therefore, balancing fluidity is critical to achieving maximum Mn recovery and minimal loss during refining. Fig. 8 Mn recovery and loss plotted against final slag viscosity

sections.heading: Empirical Analysis of Mn Loss
Industrial Implications
paragraphs: The following suggestions obtained by this study offer significant implications for sustainable and cost-effective steel production ,  particularly in the alloying of medium- and high-Mn steels during ladle refining:

sections.heading: Enhanced Mn Yield
paragraphs: It can be said from Fig.  7 c and d that by optimizing slag composition (CaO/SiO 2  = 2) and properly controlling aluminum addition, Mn recovery efficiencies of up to 68% can be achieved. This directly improves the raw material utilization and reduces Mn losses via the slag and through volatilisation, which are major issues in conventional steelmaking. Moreover, during silicothermic smelting [ 10 ], 40% of the Mn can be lost to the slag, while additional evaporation losses are unavoidable due to the high-Mn vapor pressure. In this context, the direct alloying approach explored here not only reduces the number of processing steps but also demonstrates superior Mn recovery efficiency compared with conventional ferroalloy-based steelmaking.

sections.heading: Slag Design for Mn Direct Alloying
paragraphs: The finding that Al 2 O 3 -rich slags suppress Mn volatilization and increase Mn recovery in the steel highlights a new strategy to design slag composition to balance reactivity and mass transfer (slag viscosity). Further, the formation of spinel (MgAl 2 O 4 ) in liquid slag at low basicity signifies, the importance of selection of slag and refractories to control the Mn loss due to entrapment in slag. Therefore, the present study enhanced the knowledge on slag design to conduct further trials at higher scales for direct Mn alloying into the liquid steel.

sections.heading: Process Optimization via Empirical Model
paragraphs: The empirical equation obtained in this study enables prediction of Mn loss during Mn direct alloying practice based on key parameters (e.g., amount of added Al and slag basicity), allowing for fine-tuning of process refining conditions.

sections.heading: Potential for Desulfurization in Ladle Refining
paragraphs: Although desulfurization was not explicitly investigated in the present experiments, the aluminothermic reduction environment developed in this study is inherently favorable for desulfurization. In ladle refining, the strong oxygen affinity of Al promotes the formation of Al 2 O 3 , which decreases the oxygen potential of the steel by reducing MnO and therefore enhances the thermodynamic driving force for sulfur transfer from the metal to the slag. Additionally, the slag compositions examined in this study—particularly those enriched in CaO—are known to exhibit high sulfide capacity under reducing conditions. These features indicate that the proposed Mn alloying practice could favors desulfurization process. This expands the industrial relevance of the present process and highlights its potential applicability for sustainable secondary steelmaking operations. As the scope of future work, influence of Mn direct alloying on desulfurization will be investigated in detail.

sections.heading: Sustainable Alloying Practice
paragraphs: This study highlights the potential of aluminothermic reduction of MnO as a sustainable alloying strategy for high-Mn steels. Unlike traditional ferroalloy-based alloying, which consumes large amounts of energy and generates significant CO 2  emissions, direct reduction within the ladle offers improved Mn recovery, reduced carbon intensity, and greater process efficiency. The present work provides actionable insights toward designing alloying practices that support the steel industry’s transition toward low-carbon and resource-efficient production pathways.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: A direct alloying method for Mn steel via. the aluminothermic reduction of MnO from CaO–SiO 2 –MgO–Al 2 O 3 -based ladle furnace slags. The main conclusions are as follows: The presence of 30% Al 2 O 3  in the MgO-saturated slag played a critical role in suppressing Mn volatilization by lowering the MnO activity and increasing slag viscosity compared to Al 2 O 3 -free systems, thereby suppressing the Mn loss. Aluminate-rich slags also increase the viscosity of slag and hence higher Mn retention in both the metal and slag. Formation of solid spinel phases (MgAl 2 O 4 ) in the MgO-saturated slag with low basicity (1) increases the slag viscosity and therefore entrap the Mn-rich droplet. This phenomenon is enhanced during addition of more Mn for the case of 8 masss% Mn in steel. Increasing the slag basicity from 1 to 2 reduces the viscosity which minimizes the Mn-rich droplet entrapment and interfacial resistance for settling, thus improving Mn recovery for both the 4% and 8% Mn targets. Increasing the stoichiometric addition of aluminum increases the MnO reduction and recovery of Mn in metal. Maximum recovery of Mn ~ 68% achieved from slag with basicity 2 and 2.5 times stochiometric addition of Al for a target Mn level of 8 mass%. However, adding Al beyond the stoichiometric requirement increases Mn loss due to localized overheating, which enhances vaporization, and droplet entrapment in the slag, particularly in low basicity slags. In general, the recovery of Mn in metal is sensitive to slag viscosity. The maximum recovery is observed for the slag with viscosity around 0.10 to 0.12 Pa·s. At higher and lower viscosities, Mn retention decreased. An empirical equation was derived to predict Mn loss as a function of process variables including Mn distribution ratio, basicity, Al 2 O 3  content in slag, and Al in steel after reaction. It was confirmed from this equation that the addition of excess Al promotes Mn loss, while higher basicity, Al 2 O 3  content, and Mn distribution ratio suppress it.
